questions.content:
A driving-school car of mass 1200 kg travels along a straight, dry test track at 20 m/s. The driver sees a red light and the brakes are applied. The driver's reaction time is 0.70 s. During braking, a constant braking force brings the car to rest in a braking distance of 25 m. Use g = 10 N/kg where needed.

(a) Calculate the thinking distance (the distance travelled during the reaction time). (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the kinetic energy of the car before braking, and use it to determine the average braking force. (3 marks)
(c) Calculate the deceleration of the car during braking. (2 marks)
(d) Determine the total stopping distance. (1 mark)
(e) Explain why the stopping distance of the same car is greater on a wet road. (2 marks)
(f) Predict the braking distance if the car had been travelling at 40 m/s with the same braking force. Justify your answer using energy. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: distance = speed x time = 20 x 0.70
[1] 14 m (unit required).
Common error: using 25 m or dividing speed by time.
(b)
[1] Method: KE = 1/2 x m x v^2 = 0.5 x 1200 x 20^2
[1] 240 000 J (accept 240 kJ).
[1] Work done = force x distance, so F = 240 000 / 25 = 9600 N. ECF from the KE value.
Common error: using v instead of v^2, or using the thinking distance.
(c)
[1] Method: a = F / m = 9600 / 1200 (ECF from (b))
[1] 8 m/s^2 (unit required; the deceleration is 8 m/s^2 in the direction opposite to motion). Accept the sign as negative.
(d)
[1] 14 + 25 = 39 m. ECF from (a).
(e)
[1] Less friction (grip) between tyres and road, so the maximum braking force is smaller.
[1] A smaller braking force means a smaller deceleration, so the car needs a longer distance to lose its kinetic energy. Accept: longer time to stop.
(f)
[1] KE is proportional to v^2, so doubling the speed gives 4 times the kinetic energy (960 000 J).
[1] Same force, so work done = F x d needs 4 times the distance: 4 x 25 = 100 m.
Common error: doubling the distance to 50 m.

questions.content:
Leon wants to find out how the angle of a ramp affects the speed of a trolley at the bottom of the ramp. He has a smooth wooden board, books to raise one end, a protractor, a metre ruler, a toy trolley, a stopwatch, a light gate connected to a data logger, and a small plastic crash tray.

(a) State the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables for this investigation. (3 marks)
(b) Write a testable hypothesis for the investigation and justify it using ideas about energy. (2 marks)
(c) Design a method Leon could use. Your method should include the range of angles, how the dependent variable is measured and how reliability is improved. (4 marks)
(d) Identify one safety risk in this investigation and state a precaution. (1 mark)
(e) Leon's friend suggests timing the trolley with a stopwatch instead of using the light gate. Explain why this would reduce the validity of the results. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Independent variable: angle of the ramp.
[1] Dependent variable: speed of the trolley at the bottom (accept: speed measured by the light gate).
[1] Any two control variables: mass of trolley, length of ramp, starting position, same surface/board, release method (two needed for the mark; award the mark for two correct, no mark for one).
Do not accept "the trolley" or "the ramp" alone.
(b)
[1] Hypothesis stated as a relationship: as the angle increases, the speed at the bottom increases.
[1] Justification: a steeper ramp means the trolley starts at a greater height, so it has more gravitational potential energy, which becomes more kinetic energy (v is larger).
(c)
[1] Range and interval of angles: at least five angles, for example 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 degrees, set with the protractor.
[1] Release from rest from the same marked point each time, with the light gate at the bottom measuring the speed (a card of known length fixed to the trolley passes through the gate: speed = card length / time blocked).
[1] Repeat each angle at least three times.
[1] Calculate a mean for each angle (and identify and discard anomalies), then plot speed against angle.
(d)
[1] Risk: trolley falling off the bench or books falling. Precaution: use the crash tray, keep feet clear, secure the books or stand back. Any sensible matched pair.
(e)
[1] Human reaction time (about 0.2 s) is large compared with the short time the trolley takes to pass the finish.
[1] This causes random and systematic timing errors, so the measured speeds would not reflect the true effect of the angle (not a fair test of the question). Accept: the light gate is more precise.

questions.content:
A roller-coaster car and its passengers have a total mass of 600 kg. The car is released from rest at the top of the first hill, which is 40 m above the ground. At the bottom of the hill, at ground level, the speed of the car is measured as 24 m/s. Use g = 10 N/kg.

(a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the car at the top of the hill. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the kinetic energy of the car at the bottom of the hill. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the energy dissipated during the descent and state what happens to this energy. (2 marks)
(d) Calculate the percentage of the original energy that is transferred to kinetic energy. (1 mark)
(e) Explain why the second hill of the ride must be lower than the first hill. (2 marks)
(f) Suggest one change to the design of the track or car that would reduce the energy dissipated. (1 mark)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: GPE = m x g x h = 600 x 10 x 40
[1] 240 000 J (accept 240 kJ). Unit required.
(b)
[1] Method: KE = 1/2 x m x v^2 = 0.5 x 600 x 24^2
[1] 172 800 J. Unit required.
Common error: using 24 instead of 24^2.
(c)
[1] 240 000 - 172 800 = 67 200 J. ECF from (a) and (b).
[1] Transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy (and some sound) because of friction and air resistance. Accept: heat.
(d)
[1] 172 800 / 240 000 x 100 = 72%. ECF.
(e)
[1] Some energy is dissipated as thermal energy on every part of the track, so the car has less total mechanical energy later in the ride.
[1] The car could not reach a height with more GPE than it started with; it needs a lower hill so that its remaining energy can lift it over the top (energy cannot be created).
(f)
[1] Any one: lubricate the wheels and track, use smoother bearings, give the car a more streamlined shape, reduce the mass of the car. Accept any sensible reduction of friction or air resistance.

questions.content:
A student builds a circuit for a model workshop. A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected to an 8.0 ohm resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 20 ohm resistor and a 30 ohm resistor.

(a) Calculate the combined resistance of the 20 ohm and 30 ohm resistors in parallel. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the total resistance of the circuit. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the current drawn from the battery. (1 mark)
(d) Calculate the potential difference across the 8.0 ohm resistor. (1 mark)
(e) Calculate the current in the 30 ohm resistor. (2 marks)
(f) Calculate the total electrical energy transferred by the circuit in 5.0 minutes. (2 marks)
(g) Explain why the sockets in a house are wired in parallel rather than in series. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: 1/R = 1/20 + 1/30 (or product over sum: 20 x 30 / 50)
[1] R = 12 ohms (unit required).
Common error: adding 20 + 30 = 50, which is larger than either resistor; a parallel total must be smaller than the smallest branch.
(b)
[1] 12 + 8.0 = 20 ohms. ECF from (a).
(c)
[1] I = V / R = 12 / 20 = 0.60 A. ECF from (b).
(d)
[1] V = I x R = 0.60 x 8.0 = 4.8 V. ECF from (c).
(e)
[1] Potential difference across the parallel part = 12 - 4.8 = 7.2 V. ECF from (d).
[1] I = 7.2 / 30 = 0.24 A. ECF.
(f)
[1] Method: energy = V x I x t = 12 x 0.60 x 300 (time converted to seconds)
[1] 2160 J. ECF from (c). Common error: using 5 for the time (gives 36 J).
(g)
[1] Each appliance receives the full mains potential difference.
[1] Each appliance can be switched on or off independently of the others.
[1] If one appliance or branch fails or is switched off, the others still work (in series, the current stops for all). Accept: total current is shared so wires can carry the current needed.

questions.content:
A research boat uses sonar to map the seabed. The sonar sends a pulse of ultrasound of frequency 50 000 Hz straight down. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s. The boat travels in a straight line and the time taken for the echo to return is recorded at five positions.

Position 1: 0.40 s
Position 2: 0.46 s
Position 3: 0.52 s
Position 4: 0.50 s
Position 5: 0.44 s

(a) Calculate the depth of the seabed at Position 1. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the wavelength of the ultrasound pulse in seawater. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the depth at Position 3. (1 mark)
(d) The depths at Positions 2, 4 and 5 are 345 m, 375 m and 330 m. Describe the pattern in the depth of the seabed along the boat's path and state the position of the deepest point. (2 marks)
(e) Explain why a human cannot hear this pulse. (1 mark)
(f) The sound pulse passes into a layer of colder water where its speed is lower. The frequency stays the same. State and explain what happens to the wavelength. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: depth = speed x time / 2 = 1500 x 0.40 / 2 (the echo travels down and back)
[1] 300 m (unit required).
Common error: forgetting to halve the time, which gives 600 m.
(b)
[1] Method: wavelength = speed / frequency = 1500 / 50 000
[1] 0.030 m (accept 3.0 cm). Unit required.
(c)
[1] 1500 x 0.52 / 2 = 390 m.
(d)
[1] The seabed gets deeper from Position 1 to Position 3 (300 m to 390 m), then gets shallower again (375 m, 330 m).
[1] Deepest point at Position 3 (390 m).
(e)
[1] The frequency of 50 000 Hz is above the upper limit of human hearing (about 20 000 Hz), so it is ultrasound.
(f)
[1] The wavelength decreases.
[1] Wavelength = speed / frequency, and with the same frequency a lower speed gives a shorter wavelength.

questions.content:
Nia investigates the specific heat capacity of an aluminium block of mass 0.50 kg. She places an electric heater rated at 12 V and 5.0 A into a hole in the block, with a thermometer in a second hole. She switches the heater on and records the temperature every minute. The block is not insulated.

Time (s): 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300
Temperature (degrees Celsius): 20.0, 27.5, 35.2, 42.6, 50.4, 58.0

The accepted value for the specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/kg/degree Celsius.

(a) Calculate the electrical energy supplied by the heater in 300 s. (2 marks)
(b) State the temperature rise of the block during the experiment. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium from Nia's data. (2 marks)
(d) Calculate the percentage error of Nia's value compared with the accepted value. (2 marks)
(e) Explain why Nia's value is higher than the accepted value. (2 marks)
(f) Suggest one improvement to the experiment to reduce this error. (1 mark)
(g) Predict the temperature rise if the same heater were used for 300 s on a 1.00 kg block of aluminium. Justify your answer. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: energy = power x time = 12 x 5.0 x 300 (power = 60 W)
[1] 18 000 J (accept 18 kJ). Unit required.
(b)
[1] 58.0 - 20.0 = 38.0 degrees Celsius.
(c)
[1] Method: c = Q / (m x temperature change) = 18 000 / (0.50 x 38.0). ECF from (a) and (b).
[1] 947 J/kg/degree Celsius (accept 950 or 947.4). Unit required.
(d)
[1] Method: percentage error = (measured - accepted) / accepted x 100 = (947 - 900) / 900 x 100. ECF from (c).
[1] 5.3% (accept 5.2% to 5.3%).
Common error: dividing by the measured value (gives 5.0%).
(e)
[1] Some of the heater's energy is transferred to the surroundings (the block is not insulated) instead of heating the block.
[1] The calculation assumes all 18 000 J raised the temperature, so the energy used in the calculation is too large and c appears too high. Accept: the temperature rise is smaller than it should be.
(f)
[1] Wrap the block in insulation (for example, a layer of foam or a lid), so less energy is lost.
(g)
[1] Temperature rise would be halved to about 19 degrees Celsius.
[1] The same energy is shared by twice the mass; temperature change = Q / (m x c), so it is inversely proportional to mass. ECF from (c).

questions.content:
Technetium-99m is a radioactive isotope used in hospitals as a medical tracer. A patient is injected with a dose of Technetium-99m that has an initial activity of 480 MBq (megabecquerels) in a gamma camera scan. The half-life of Technetium-99m is 6.0 hours. It emits gamma radiation.

(a) State what is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the activity of the dose 12 hours after the injection. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the time taken for the activity to fall to 15 MBq. (2 marks)
(d) Explain why Technetium-99m is suitable as a medical tracer. (3 marks)
(e) Explain why an alpha-emitting isotope would not be suitable for this scan. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] The time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay (or for the activity to fall to half of its original value).
(b)
[1] 12 hours is 2 half-lives.
[1] 480 to 240 to 120, so 120 MBq (unit required).
Common error: halving only once (240 MBq) or dividing by 12.
(c)
[1] Halving 480 to 240 to 120 to 60 to 30 to 15 takes 5 half-lives.
[1] 5 x 6.0 = 30 hours.
(d)
[1] Gamma rays are highly penetrating, so they pass out of the body and can be detected by the gamma camera.
[1] The half-life is short (6 hours), so the activity falls quickly and the patient's exposure to radiation is limited.
[1] Enough activity remains for the scan period; it is not stored in the body long term. Accept: low risk of damage to cells.
(e)
[1] Alpha particles are stopped by a few centimetres of air or by skin/tissue, so they would not leave the body to be detected.
[1] Alpha radiation is strongly ionising, so inside the body it would cause damage to cells.

questions.content:
Priya investigates how the number of turns of wire on an electromagnet affects the number of paper clips the magnet can lift. She wraps insulated wire around an iron nail, connects it to a 6.0 V power supply and counts how many paper clips the nail lifts at once. She repeats each test three times.

Number of turns (clips lifted in trial 1, trial 2, trial 3):
10 turns: 3, 4, 3
20 turns: 7, 7, 8
30 turns: 11, 12, 11
40 turns: 14, 15, 15
50 turns: 20, 21, 12

(a) Calculate the mean number of clips lifted by 30 turns. Give your answer to one decimal place. (1 mark)
(b) Identify the anomalous result and justify your choice. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the mean for 50 turns, leaving out the anomalous result. (1 mark)
(d) Write a conclusion for the investigation, supported by data and scientific reasoning. (3 marks)
(e) State one safety precaution Priya should take when the wire is connected for a long time. (1 mark)
(f) Design one change to Priya's method that would give more precise results than counting clips, and explain how it improves precision. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] (11 + 12 + 11) / 3 = 11.3 clips.
(b)
[1] 12 clips at 50 turns (trial 3).
[1] It does not fit the pattern of the other two repeats (20 and 21) and the trend that more turns lift more clips; it is far from the other readings.
(c)
[1] (20 + 21) / 2 = 20.5 clips.
(d)
[1] As the number of turns increases, the mean number of clips lifted increases (3.3 at 10 turns, 20.5 at 50 turns).
[1] Data support: the increase is roughly proportional, about 0.4 extra clips for each extra turn.
[1] Scientific reason: more turns give a stronger magnetic field around the iron core for the same current, so the magnet exerts a larger force.
(e)
[1] The wire and nail heat up, so disconnect the supply between tests or wait for it to cool, and avoid touching the wire. Accept: use a lower current or switch off between readings.
(f)
[1] Use a newton meter (or balance) to measure the force needed to pull the magnet away from a steel plate, or increase the mass lifted using small standard masses.
[1] This gives a continuous measurement instead of whole clips, so smaller changes can be detected (higher resolution). Accept: a data logger with a magnetic field sensor.

questions.content:
A coastal region is planning an offshore wind farm. The wind farm will have 40 turbines. Each turbine has a rated power of 5.0 MW. Because the wind speed varies, the farm actually delivers an average of 40% of its rated power over a year. A year has 8760 hours. An average home in the region uses 3.5 MWh of electricity per year. A gas power station would release 0.40 kg of carbon dioxide for each kWh (kilowatt-hour) of electricity generated. 1 MWh = 1000 kWh.

(a) Calculate the total rated power of the wind farm. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the average power output of the wind farm. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the energy generated in one year, in MWh. (2 marks)
(d) Estimate how many homes this energy could supply. Give your answer to two significant figures. (2 marks)
(e) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in tonnes, that would be avoided each year if this energy replaced electricity from the gas power station. (1 tonne = 1000 kg) (2 marks)
(f) Evaluate the proposal. Discuss two benefits and two concerns, and make a justified judgement about whether the wind farm should go ahead. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] 40 x 5.0 = 200 MW.
(b)
[1] 0.40 x 200 = 80 MW. ECF from (a).
(c)
[1] Method: energy = power x time = 80 x 8760
[1] 700 800 MWh. ECF from (b). Unit required.
(d)
[1] Method: 700 800 / 3.5 = 200 229 homes. ECF from (c).
[1] About 200 000 homes (2 significant figures). Common error: leaving the answer at 6 significant figures or rounding to 20 000.
(e)
[1] Method: 700 800 MWh = 700 800 000 kWh; x 0.40 = 280 320 000 kg
[1] About 280 000 tonnes (accept 2.8 x 10^5 tonnes). ECF from (c).
Common error: forgetting to convert MWh to kWh or kg to tonnes.
(f)
[1] Two benefits: any two of: no carbon dioxide released during operation; renewable source; lower long-term fuel costs; local jobs; improved energy security.
[1] Two concerns: any two of: effect on seabirds and marine life; visual impact or noise; high construction cost; output varies with the wind so back-up or storage is needed.
[1] Reasoned judgement that weighs the benefits against the concerns, using the data (for example, the large carbon dioxide saving and the homes supplied).
[1] Consideration of limitations or conditions: for example, the 40% average is an assumption; mitigation such as studies of bird paths; storage to deal with variable supply. Accept any other evaluation that is balanced and justified.
